A research task. Do not ask for design approval, do not run any brainstorming or approval
workflow. Proceed directly to work.

TARGET. The referee listed five routes, any one of which would be a substantial further
improvement, and said what unites them: they "would make the mechanism itself, rather than
one highly successful implementation of it, the central theorem." His first, and the same
thing he originally named as option (b) of the tier threshold, is:

  an abstract kernel theorem encompassing stable, Gaussian, Poisson, and other
  polynomial-tail kernels.

Pursue that.

FRAME IT AS AN ABSTRACTION, NOT A GENERALISATION SWEEP. The productive question is not
"can we redo the proof for more kernels one at a time", it is: WHICH PROPERTIES OF THE
KERNEL DOES THE MECHANISM ACTUALLY USE? Go through the existing argument for the stable
kernel - Theorem 4.27, the standalone two-background KL perturbation lemma, the proxy
positivity and normalization, the o(s^{-r}) background estimates, the Hessian
identification, the cubic remainder - and extract the minimal hypotheses on the smoothing
kernel that each step genuinely requires. Candidates to check, not to assume: bounded
gradient of log p_1, L^1 translation continuity, the moment-mode expansion structure, decay
or regular variation of the tail, and whatever makes the retained common jet well defined.

Then state and prove an abstract theorem under exactly those hypotheses, and verify
membership for the concrete cases:
  - isotropic alpha-stable, 0 < alpha < 2, which must reduce to the existing theorem;
  - Gaussian, which the paper currently excludes (alpha = 2) - say clearly whether the
    abstract hypotheses cover it, and if so what the statement gives there, and if not,
    exactly which hypothesis fails;
  - Poisson;
  - at least one further polynomial-tail kernel.

A clean, minimal hypothesis set with three or four verified members is worth far more than
a broad-sounding theorem with one member.

HONEST OUTCOMES, in order of value:
 1. An abstract theorem with minimal hypotheses and several verified members.
 2. An abstract theorem whose hypotheses are honest but which only one or two known kernels
    satisfy - state that plainly, and say which natural kernels fail and at which step.
 3. A precise identification of the obstruction: the mechanism does NOT abstract, and here
    is the step that is irreducibly stable-specific. State this in the FIRST LINE of your
    report if it is the outcome. This is a real result and is much more valuable than a
    vacuous abstraction.

Do NOT produce a theorem whose hypotheses are simply a restatement of "the stable kernel
works", i.e. a hypothesis list assembled by reading off what the stable proof needed and
that no other kernel is shown to satisfy. That is the failure mode here, and the referee
will see it immediately - he caught the analogous risk on the admissible class last round
and asked whether it was gerrymandered.

RULES:
 - Every claim proved at referee standard. Numerics are sanity checks and never substitute
   for proof.
 - Do not weaken, restate or renumber any existing theorem. Theorem 4.27 and Corollaries
   4.28, 4.29 keep their numbers; leave new results unnumbered if that preserves numbering.
 - Do not touch the venue or priority wording, and do not reinstate any canonicity or
   uniqueness language.
 - Keep every .tex under 800 lines; split if needed.
 - Alternating clean rebuild with .aux removed: latexmk -pdfxe exit 0, zero undefined
   references, citations and multiply-defined labels in both documents.
 - Re-run every artifacts/verify*.py and artifacts/test_*.py; report pass counts. Any
   archived output must stay deterministic - no wall-clock timings, two consecutive runs
   byte-identical. Regenerate artifacts/SHA256SUMS (LF) if artifacts change and confirm zero
   failures from the artifacts directory.
 - No revision marks anywhere.

REPORT: the minimal hypothesis set; which of stable, Gaussian, Poisson and your fourth
kernel satisfy it, with the verification for each; for any that fail, the exact step that
fails; whether the stable case reduces to Theorem 4.27 as it must; page and theorem counts
before and after; and compile and test results.

# PDF Skill

## When to use
- Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
- Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
- Validate final rendering before delivery.

## Workflow
1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
   - Use `pdftoppm` if available.
   - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
3. Use `pdfplumber` (or `pypdf`) for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on it for layout fidelity.
4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.

## Temp and output conventions
- Use `tmp/pdfs/` for intermediate files; delete when done.
- Write final artifacts under `output/pdf/` when working in this repo.
- Keep filenames stable and descriptive.

## Dependencies (install if missing)
Prefer `uv` for dependency management.

Python packages:
```
uv pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```
If `uv` is unavailable:
```
python3 -m pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```
System tools (for rendering):
```
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install poppler

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install -y poppler-utils
```

If installation isn't possible in this environment, tell the user which dependency is missing and how to install it locally.

## Environment
No required environment variables.

## Rendering command
```
pdftoppm -png $INPUT_PDF $OUTPUT_PREFIX
```

## Quality expectations
- Maintain polished visual design: consistent typography, spacing, margins, and section hierarchy.
- Avoid rendering issues: clipped text, overlapping elements, broken tables, black squares, or unreadable glyphs.
- Charts, tables, and images must be sharp, aligned, and clearly labeled.
- Use ASCII hyphens only. Avoid U+2011 (non-breaking hyphen) and other Unicode dashes.
- Citations and references must be human-readable; never leave tool tokens or placeholder strings.

## Final checks
- Do not deliver until the latest PNG inspection shows zero visual or formatting defects.
- Confirm headers/footers, page numbering, and section transitions look polished.
- Keep intermediate files organized or remove them after final approval.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans â€” one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** â€” never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code â€” the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in every step â€” if a step changes code, show the code
- Exact commands with expected output
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself â€” not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags â€” any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review â€” just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

# Verification Before Completion

## Overview

Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency.

**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.

**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
```

If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.

## The Gate Function

```
BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:

1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim

Skip any step = lying, not verifying
```

## Common Failures

| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |

## Red Flags - STOP

- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
- About to commit/push/PR without verification
- Trusting agent success reports
- Relying on partial verification
- Thinking "just this once"
- Tired and wanting work over
- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**

## Rationalization Prevention

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
| "I'm confident" | Confidence â‰  evidence |
| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
| "Linter passed" | Linter â‰  compiler |
| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion â‰  excuse |
| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |

## Key Patterns

**Tests:**
```
âœ… [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
âŒ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
```

**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
```
âœ… Write â†’ Run (pass) â†’ Revert fix â†’ Run (MUST FAIL) â†’ Restore â†’ Run (pass)
âŒ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
```

**Build:**
```
âœ… [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
âŒ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
```

**Requirements:**
```
âœ… Re-read plan â†’ Create checklist â†’ Verify each â†’ Report gaps or completion
âŒ "Tests pass, phase complete"
```

**Agent delegation:**
```
âœ… Agent reports success â†’ Check VCS diff â†’ Verify changes â†’ Report actual state
âŒ Trust agent report
```

## Why This Matters

From 24 failure memories:
- your human partner said "I don't believe you" - trust broken
- Undefined functions shipped - would crash
- Missing requirements shipped - incomplete features
- Time wasted on false completion â†’ redirect â†’ rework
- Violates: "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced."

## When To Apply

**ALWAYS before:**
- ANY variation of success/completion claims
- ANY expression of satisfaction
- ANY positive statement about work state
- Committing, PR creation, task completion
- Moving to next task
- Delegating to agents

**Rule applies to:**
- Exact phrases
- Paraphrases and synonyms
- Implications of success
- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness

## The Bottom Line

**No shortcuts for verification.**

Run the command. Read the output. THEN claim the result.

This is non-negotiable.

- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
- About to commit/push/PR without verification
- Trusting agent success reports
- Relying on partial verification
- Thinking "just this once"
- Tired and wanting work over
- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**

## Rationalization Prevention

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
| "I'm confident" | Confidence â‰  evidence |
| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
| "Linter passed" | Linter â‰  compiler |
| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion â‰  excuse |
| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |

## Key Patterns

**Tests:**
```
âœ… [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
âŒ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
```

**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
```
âœ… Write â†’ Run (pass) â†’ Revert fix â†’ Run (MUST FAIL) â†’ Restore â†’ Run (pass)
âŒ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
```

**Build:**
```
âœ… [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
âŒ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
```

**Requirements:**
```
âœ… Re-read plan â†’ Create checklist â†’ Verify each â†’ Report gaps or completion
âŒ "Tests pass, phase complete"
```

**Agent delegation:**
```
âœ… Agent reports success â†’ Check VCS diff â†’ Verify changes â†’ Report actual state
âŒ Trust agent report
```

## Why This Matters

From 24 failure memories:
- your human partner said "I don't believe you" - trust broken
- Undefined functions shipped - would crash
- Missing requirements shipped - incomplete features
- Time wasted on false completion â†’ redirect â†’ rework
- Violates: "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced."

## When To Apply

**ALWAYS before:**
- ANY variation of success/completion claims
- ANY expression of satisfaction
- ANY positive statement about work state
- Committing, PR creation, task completion
- Moving to next task
- Delegating to agents

**Rule applies to:**
- Exact phrases
- Paraphrases and synonyms
- Implications of success
- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness

## The Bottom Line

**No shortcuts for verification.**

Run the command. Read the output. THEN claim the result.

This is non-negotiable.

   1: \begin{unnumberedlemma}[Two-background KL perturbation]
   2: Let \((E,\Omega)\) be a probability space and let
   3: \(\epsilon_s\downarrow0\).  For \(i=1,2\), let \(A_{i,s}\) be probability
   4: densities such that, for one constant \(c>0\) and all sufficiently large
   5: \(s\),
   6: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-two-background-hypotheses}
   7:  A_{i,s}\ge c,\qquad
   8:  \|A_{i,s}-1\|_1=o(1),\qquad
   9:  \|A_{1,s}-A_{2,s}\|_1=o(\epsilon_s).
  10: \end{equation}
  11: Let \(U_{i,s}=\epsilon_sB_{i,s}\), where
  12: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-two-background-modes}
  13:  \sup_s\bigl(\|B_{1,s}\|_\infty+\|B_{2,s}\|_\infty\bigr)<\infty,
  14:  \qquad \int B_{i,s}\dd\Omega=0.
  15: \end{equation}
  16: Suppose
  17: \[
  18:  q_{i,s}=A_{i,s}+U_{i,s}+R_{i,s}
  19: \]
  20: are probability densities, uniformly bounded below by a positive constant,
  21: and
  22: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-two-background-remainders}
  23:  \|R_{i,s}\|_\infty+\|R_{i,s}\|_1=o(\epsilon_s).
  24: \end{equation}
  25: Assume also that
  26: \(\int A_{1,s}\log^+A_{1,s}\dd\Omega<\infty\) for every sufficiently
  27: large \(s\).  Then all relative entropies below are finite and
  28: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-two-background-conclusion}
  29:  D_{\rm KL}(q_{1,s}\Omega\|q_{2,s}\Omega)
  30:  =D_{\rm KL}(A_{1,s}\Omega\|A_{2,s}\Omega)
  31:  +\frac{\epsilon_s^2}{2}
  32:    \int(B_{1,s}-B_{2,s})^2\dd\Omega+o(\epsilon_s^2).
  33: \end{equation}
  34: \end{unnumberedlemma}
  35: 
  36: \begin{proof}
  37: Suppress \(s\), write \(P_i=A_i+U_i\), and put
  38: \[
  39:  f(a,b)=a\log(a/b)-a+b.
  40: \]
  41: For large \(s\), \(P_i\ge c/2\).  Since both \(P_i\) and \(q_i\) are
  42: bounded below, the segments \(P_i+tR_i\), \(0\le t\le1\), have a common
  43: positive lower bound.  On any such region,
  44: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-two-background-first-partials}
  45:  f_a(a,b)=\log(a/b),\qquad f_b(a,b)=1-a/b,
  46:  \qquad |f_a(a,b)|+|f_b(a,b)|\le C|a-b|.
  47: \end{equation}
  48: The mean-value theorem and
  49: \[
  50:  |(P_1+tR_1)-(P_2+tR_2)|
  51:  \le |A_1-A_2|+|U_1-U_2|+|R_1|+|R_2|
  52: \]
  53: therefore give the explicit remainder-removal bound
  54: \begin{align}
  55:  &\left|\int f(q_1,q_2)\dd\Omega-
  56:               \int f(P_1,P_2)\dd\Omega\right|\notag\\
  57:  &\quad\le
  58:  C(\|R_1\|_\infty+\|R_2\|_\infty)\|A_1-A_2\|_1\notag\\
  59:  &\qquad+C(\|U_1\|_\infty+\|U_2\|_\infty)
  60:           (\|R_1\|_1+\|R_2\|_1)\notag\\
  61:  &\qquad+C(\|R_1\|_\infty+\|R_2\|_\infty)
  62:           (\|R_1\|_1+\|R_2\|_1)
  63:  =o(\epsilon_s^2).
  64:  \label{eq:abstract-two-background-remove-remainders}
  65: \end{align}
  66: 
  67: It remains to expand the two positive backgrounds.  Set
  68: \[
  69:  a_t=A_1+tU_1,\qquad b_t=A_2+tU_2,
  70:  \qquad H(t)=\int f(a_t,b_t)\dd\Omega.
  71: \]
  72: The zero-mean condition in \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-modes} makes
  73: \(a_t\) and \(b_t\) probability densities.  The four quantities used in
  74: Taylor's formula are, explicitly,
  75: \begin{align}
  76:  H(0)&=D_{\rm KL}(A_1\Omega\|A_2\Omega),
  77:  \label{eq:abstract-two-background-H-zero}\\
  78:  H'(t)&=\int\left\{U_1\log\frac{a_t}{b_t}
  79:             +U_2\left(1-\frac{a_t}{b_t}\right)\right\}\dd\Omega,
  80:  \label{eq:abstract-two-background-H-first}\\
  81:  H''(t)&=\int\left\{\frac{U_1^2}{a_t}
  82:        -\frac{2U_1U_2}{b_t}+\frac{a_tU_2^2}{b_t^2}\right\}\dd\Omega,
  83:  \label{eq:abstract-two-background-H-second}\\
  84:  H'''(t)&=\int\left\{-\frac{U_1^3}{a_t^2}
  85:        +\frac{3U_1U_2^2}{b_t^2}
  86:        -\frac{2a_tU_2^3}{b_t^3}\right\}\dd\Omega.
  87:  \label{eq:abstract-two-background-H-third}
  88: \end{align}
  89: These formulas follow by direct differentiation; the estimates below also
  90: provide an integrable majorant and hence justify differentiation under the
  91: integral.
  92: 
  93: At \(t=0\), the two coefficients in \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-H-first}
  94: are bounded by \(C|A_1-A_2|\).  Thus
  95: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-two-background-first-variation}
  96:  |H'(0)|\le
  97:  C(\|U_1\|_\infty+\|U_2\|_\infty)\|A_1-A_2\|_1
  98:  =o(\epsilon_s^2).
  99: \end{equation}
 100: For the Hessian, the lower bound in
 101: \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-hypotheses} gives
 102: \begin{align}
 103:  \left\|\frac1{A_i}-1\right\|_1
 104:  &\le c^{-1}\|A_i-1\|_1=o(1),
 105:  \label{eq:abstract-two-background-inverse-coefficient}\\
 106:  \left\|\frac{A_1}{A_2^2}-1\right\|_1
 107:  &\le c^{-2}\|A_1-A_2\|_1
 108:       +c^{-1}\|A_2-1\|_1=o(1).
 109:  \label{eq:abstract-two-background-third-coefficient}
 110: \end{align}
 111: Indeed, the second line uses
 112: \(A_1/A_2^2-1=(A_1-A_2)/A_2^2+(1/A_2-1)\).
 113: Since \(\|U_i\|_\infty=O(\epsilon_s)\), these coefficient estimates in
 114: \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-H-second} yield
 115: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-two-background-hessian-limit}
 116:  H''(0)=\int(U_1-U_2)^2\dd\Omega+o(\epsilon_s^2)
 117:  =\epsilon_s^2\int(B_{1,s}-B_{2,s})^2\dd\Omega
 118:   +o(\epsilon_s^2).
 119: \end{equation}
 120: 
 121: Finally, \(a_t,b_t\) are uniformly bounded below and
 122: \(|U_1|+|U_2|\le C\epsilon_s\).  Formula
 123: \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-H-third} consequently gives
 124: \[
 125:  \left|\frac{\dd^3}{\dd t^3}f(a_t,b_t)\right|
 126:  \le C\epsilon_s^3(1+a_t).
 127: \]
 128: Because \(\int a_t\dd\Omega=1\),
 129: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-two-background-cubic-bound}
 130:  \sup_{0\le t\le1}|H'''(t)|\le C\epsilon_s^3
 131:  =o(\epsilon_s^2).
 132: \end{equation}
 133: Taylor's theorem, \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-first-variation},
 134: \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-hessian-limit}, and
 135: \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-cubic-bound} expand \(H(1)\).  Combining
 136: that expansion with
 137: \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-remove-remainders} proves
 138: \eqref{eq:abstract-two-background-conclusion}.  Finiteness follows from the
 139: assumed positive lower bounds, the finite positive entropy of \(A_1\), and
 140: the fact that \(U_i,R_i\) are bounded perturbations; the negative part of
 141: \(a\log(a/b)\) is bounded in absolute integral by
 142: \(e^{-1}\int b\dd\Omega=e^{-1}\).
 143: \end{proof}

  84: \def\JFAArticleMain{1}
  85: \begin{abstract}
  86: Arbitrary-order first unmatched moment relative-entropy asymptotics under
  87: Gaussian smoothing are due to Chen and Niles-Weed
  88: \cite{ChenNilesWeed2022SmoothedWasserstein}, while all-order
  89: stable/fractional heat-kernel density expansions are also prior work
  90: \cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2017,
  91: IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2022RefinedFractional}.  Neither result is claimed as
  92: new.  For the heavy-tailed isotropic strictly \(\alpha\)-stable kernels,
  93: \(0<\alpha<2\), we identify the optimal complete-moment condition that
  94: transfers the density expansion through relative entropy.
  95: If two
  96: laws on \(\RR^d\) match all tensor moments below the integer order \(r\ge1\),
  97: have a nonzero order-\(r\) difference \(\Delta_r\), and have finite
  98: \(p_{r,\alpha,d}\)th absolute moments, where
  99: \[
 100:  p_{r,\alpha,d}=\max\left\{r,
 101:  \frac{2r(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+2r}\right\},
 102: \]
 103: then
 104: \[
 105:  D_{\rm KL}(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\|p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\eta)
 106:  =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d,r}(\Delta_r)s^{-2r}+o(s^{-2r}).
 107: \]
 108: The coefficient is an orthogonally invariant positive-definite quadratic
 109: form on symmetric order-\(r\) tensors.  The endpoint moment is sufficient.
 110: When \(d+\alpha>2r\), every exponent
 111: \(\rho\in[r,p_{r,\alpha,d})\) fails uniformly even for pairs with finite
 112: nonzero \(\Delta_r\); when \(d+\alpha\le2r\), the threshold equals \(r\), and
 113: smaller exponents fail only to define \(\Delta_r\) throughout the moment
 114: class.  Thus the contribution is the heavy-tailed critical exponent,
 115: endpoint sufficiency, and uniform sharpness, not the Gaussian quadratic
 116: mechanism itself.
 117: 
 118: At every order \(r\), finite \(r\)th moments alone also give a law-by-law
 119: decomposition: the universal quadratic tensor term plus a nonnegative
 120: relative \(\Phi\)-energy between two positive proxies that retain each law's
 121: unexpanded tail beyond the smoothing scale and their common lower-order jet.
 122: To the best of our knowledge, this explicit positive proxy decomposition,
 123: with vanishing of its KL term as an exact necessary and sufficient condition
 124: for attainment of the universal coefficient, is new; no uniqueness or
 125: canonicity of the proxy is asserted.  The defect is nevertheless unchanged
 126: up to \(o(s^{-2r})\) by separate comparable hard or smooth retention profiles,
 127: by either additive or multiplicative mass normalization, and by common
 128: bounded order-\(r\) proxy gauges.  Among order-\(r\) jet-faithful proxies in
 129: the prescribed retained-tail/common-core ansatz, asymptotic coefficient
 130: rigidity identifies this gauge as the remaining freedom; no classification
 131: of all reasonable proxy conventions is claimed.
 132: For the Cauchy kernel, the Cayley
 133: transform additionally yields the exact equivalence between finite variance
 134: and bounded \(t^4\) relative entropy, an all-order finite Laurent rule for the
 135: subsequent coefficients, and a fully justified nonlocal Bregman tail identity
 136: for the moving matched quotient.
 137: \end{abstract}

 152: For \(|z|\le1\), the local quotient--Taylor estimate
 153: \eqref{eq:local-multidim-taylor-remainder} implies the first line of
 154: \eqref{eq:critical-lq-global-remainder}.  For \(|z|>1\), the exact identity
 155: gives \(\|F_\cdot(z)\|_{q_d}\le C_d|z|^{4/q_d}=C_d|z|^{p_d}\).
 156: Every coefficient of \(T_m\) is bounded in \(y\), and \(m\le p_d\), so
 157: \(\|T_m(\cdot,z)\|_{q_d}\le C_d|z|^{p_d}\).  Finally,
 158: \(m+1>p_d\), which proves the last inequality for \(|z|\le1\).
 159: \end{proof}
